new_entities.name: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation after stroke
aliases: repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for stroke rehab
new_entities.description: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation used as an adjunct to motor rehabilitation after stroke.

new_entities.name: Motor function
new_entities.description: Measured motor performance and impairment severity on validated functional scales.

edges.effect_quant: The 2020 PRISMA meta-analysis found better Fugl-Meyer motor scores with post-stroke rTMS (SMD 0.635, 95% CI 0.421-0.848), but newer stratified work suggests benefit depends on stroke stage, severity, and stimulation protocol.
edges.population: adults with motor impairment after ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke
edges.mechanism: rTMS aims to rebalance cortical excitability by dampening maladaptive interhemispheric inhibition or boosting residual excitability in the affected motor cortex. That mechanism is plausible, but the effect is protocol-sensitive, which is why pooled benefit coexists with uncertainty about who should receive which stimulation pattern.
edges.summary: The evidence base repeatedly shows a positive average effect of rTMS on post-stroke motor scales, with the clearest signal in meta-analyses pooling randomized trials. At the same time, those gains are not uniform across stroke stage or severity, so this edge is best characterized as mixed rather than universally protective.
edges.caveats: The label rTMS bundles together low-frequency, high-frequency, and theta-burst approaches applied to different hemispheres and at different timepoints after stroke. That heterogeneity is large enough that a positive pooled effect should not be mistaken for a settled one-size-fits-all protocol.

evidence.citation: Wang Y et al 2020 Am J Phys Med Rehabil
